column2: It 'pays a verbal tribute to the old confusion'; she would call 'perfect' what he calls 'pure' and make theorists state any further assumptions explicitly.

column1: Robinson 1934: two conditions for a perfect market between products A and B?
column2: All buyers alike in preferences, and each buyer deals with only one firm at a time. Then any relative price rise ends a firm's sales.

column1: Cloze: For Robinson, if there is only {{c1::one buyer}} the market for each firm must be perfect.
column2: one buyer

column1: Robinson 1934: with falling marginal costs in a perfect market, how many firms survive?
column2: Only one — price-cutting drives the other out, so competition cannot be perfect.

column1: Robinson 1934: what determines the number of firms needed for perfect competition (rising MC)?
column2: The slopes of their marginal cost curves (and elasticity of total demand): flatter MC → fewer firms needed; vertical MC → indefinitely many.

column1: What is the point of Robinson's Saturday-night fish market example?
column2: With perfectly inelastic supply competition is not strictly perfect, yet the competitive output sells at the competitive price unless demand is highly inelastic.

column1: Who replied (1937) that Robinson's argument implies 'for full perfection the requirement is bilateral monopoly'?
column2: Chamberlin, 'Monopolistic or Imperfect Competition?' QJE Aug 1937 (#63), p. 569 n.

column1: Kaldor 1935: why is Robinson's tangency result 'merely a statement of a tautology'?
column2: She includes in her cost curves profits not competed away by entry, so tangency holds by definition and implies no excess capacity.

column1: List the four (implicit) assumptions Kaldor 1935 finds behind Chamberlin's excess-capacity theory.
column2: (1) Many producers of slightly different products; (2) preferences evenly distributed; (3) no institutional monopoly, i.e. free entry; (4) economies of scale over some range.

column1: Cloze: Kaldor 1935 calls duopoly 'the {{c1::leading species of a large genus}}'.
column2: leading species of a large genus

column1: What is an 'imagined demand curve' (Kaldor)?
column2: The producer's own view of how sales respond to his price, based on expected rival and entrant reactions — determinate in his mind, unlike the indeterminate 'real' curve.

column1: Kaldor 1935: what happens with free entry and no economies of scale?
column2: Entry continues until each firm's demand is infinitely elastic: perfect competition establishes itself. 'The mathematical economists … weren't such fools after all.'

column1: Kaldor 1935: why don't economies of scale guarantee tangency?
column2: An entrant needs a minimum output, which may push all firms into losses; indivisibility shields existing profits and gives a monopolistic advantage to whoever is first in the field.

column1: Define 'institutional monopoly' (Kaldor 1935).
column2: Anything — patent, copyright, trade-mark, trade-name, unique resources, buyers' inertia — preventing a rival producing an identical product at the same relative cost.

column1: Kaldor 1935 policy footnote: what follows from a uniform taxi fare?
column2: Too many empty taxis — price agreements without output limits generate excess capacity (likewise under-employed professionals, too many tobacco shops).

column1: Which 1937 article accepted Kaldor's point that full free entry means anyone could produce an identical product?
column2: Chamberlin, 'Monopolistic or Imperfect Competition?' (#63), recording a 'change of view': free entry is incompatible with a differentiated product.

column1: Kaldor 1935 on welfare: why can't excess capacity be called consumers' choice of variety over cheapness?
column2: Consumers are never actually offered the choice between fewer varieties at lower prices and more varieties at higher prices.

column1: Kahn 1935: when is output 'ideal'?
column2: When the value of the marginal social product of each marginal unit of a factor is the same in a use as in its alternative occupation.

column1: Kahn 1935: with widespread external economies, which industries should be expanded?
column2: Those with above-average external economies (per unit increase of employment); those below the average should contract.

column1: Kahn 1935: what tacit assumption reconciles Pigou's rule with Kahn's?
column2: That external economies and diseconomies are rare, so their average is about zero (Pigou's 'archetypal industry').

column1: Cloze: 'Dr. Clapham's economic boxes were full all the time, but the economists were looking on the {{c1::wrong shelf}}.'
column2: wrong shelf (Kahn 1935, p. 13 — the boxes are public utilities/lumpy units to be subsidised)

column1: Kahn 1935: ratio of marginal revenue to price?
column2: (e − 1)/e, where e is the elasticity of demand for the individual firm; e is an inverse measure of imperfection.

column1: Kahn 1935 (irrational imperfection, factors drawn from same industry): which way should hired factors and entrepreneurs move?
column2: Opposite ways: hired factors into abnormally imperfect industries, entrepreneurs out — e.g. more labour in retailing but fewer shops.

column1: Kahn 1935: what policy device brings an industry to the 'average degree of imperfection'?
column2: A subsidy (or tax) on hired factors plus a lump-sum tax (or subsidy) per entrepreneur; at the ideal point they exactly offset.

column1: Kahn 1935: when is an entrepreneur's marginal social productivity negative?
column2: When firms produce at falling average cost of hired factors (irrational imperfection): society gains by concentrating the factors in fewer firms.

column1: Distinguish rational from irrational market imperfection (Kahn 1935).
column2: Rational: preferences reflecting real satisfactions (transport cost, lasting tastes). Irrational: from ignorance/inertia, causing no loss when the consumer is switched to another firm.

column1: Which 1937 article cited Kahn's p. 20 disclaimer that 'imperfection of competition' carries no monopoly implications?
column2: Chamberlin, 'Monopolistic or Imperfect Competition?' (#63), as evidence the imperfect-competition school treats monopoly and competition as mutually exclusive.

column1: Harrod 1936: 'the leading principle of the theory of imperfect competition'?
column2: That entrepreneurs tend to equate marginal cost to marginal revenue (criticised by Chamberlin 1937 as true under any market form).

column1: Harrod 1936: reward costs vs work costs?
column2: Reward costs = rates of pay per unit of factor; work costs = number of such units required per unit of output.

column1: Cloze: Harrod (1936) argues that in good times demand is apt to get {{c1::less elastic}} and competition more imperfect.
column2: less elastic

column1: Harrod 1936: why does the elasticity of demand fall when incomes rise?
column2: Searching for the cheapest market is a discommodity the richer buyer (or prosperous firm) can afford not to incur; habit makes buyers careless.

column1: Harrod 1936 numerical example: average elasticity rises from 4 to 5 in a recession — effect?
column2: Prices fall about 6¼ per cent and profits about 25 per cent.

column1: Chamberlin 1937: what is 'monopolistic competition'?
column2: A challenge to the view that monopoly and competition are alternatives: most situations are 'composites of both', grounded in product differentiation.

column1: Chamberlin 1937: is the large-group tangency solution central to monopolistic competition?
column2: No — it 'flows from certain heroic assumptions' and is 'mainly an expositional device', an intermediate stage of the theory.

column1: Chamberlin 1937 on increasing returns and monopolistic competition?
column2: Falling costs at equilibrium are a result, not part of the definition; increasing returns are 'neither necessary nor sufficient'. The demand curve's shape marks the contrast with pure competition.

column1: Chamberlin 1937: does a larger number of differentiated sellers make firm demand curves approach the horizontal?
column2: No general presumption: new firms may expand the area or appeal to new buyers; on a line the curve keeps its slope; numbers depend on how broadly the field is defined.

column1: Cloze: Chamberlin (1937), following Kaldor, holds that full 'freedom of entry' is quite incompatible with a {{c1::differentiated product}}.
column2: differentiated product

column1: How does Chamberlin say Robinson defines a 'monopolist', and his jibe?
column2: As any individual seller, even under perfect competition — like calling either rail of a railway a 'monorail' or a polygamist's relation with one wife 'monogamy'.

column1: Why does Chamberlin call 'imperfect competition' a 'purely negative' term?
column2: It merely admits real competition is imperfect, keeping competition and monopoly as non-overlapping categories with minimal interference to old habits of thought.

column1: Chamberlin 1937: three consequences of the monopolistic vs imperfect conception?
column2: (1) Profits — genuine monopoly profits pervade the system; (2) competitive norms — pure competition is no ideal, variety matters; (3) 'exploitation' — all factors get less than MPP×price.

column1: Chamberlin 1937: why is the entrepreneur not the 'exploiter' under monopolistic competition?
column2: All shares are paid less than the value of their marginal physical product; Robinson's argument wrongly treats entrepreneur and firm as one indivisible unit, but entrepreneurship is divisible.

column1: Date card: Chamberlin's 'Monopolistic or Imperfect Competition?' — where/when?
column2: QJE, August 1937 (vol. 51, pp. 557–580); parts given at the AEA meeting, Chicago, December 1936.

column1: Coase 1937 (Monopoly Price): what case does he examine?
column2: A combine formed from the firms of a previously perfectly competitive industry, with no new entry — Robinson's 'comparison of monopoly and competitive output'.

column1: Coase 1937: why might businessmen not set MC = MR?
column2: Cost accounts make marginal cost hard to discover, demand curves are even harder to know, and dim awareness of the rule tends to entrench the status quo price.

column1: Coase 1937: effect of uncertainty about the demand curve on monopoly price?
column2: Price is raised step by step, each step revealing a new certain point — approaching but not reaching the monopoly price.

column1: Coase 1937: monopolist who looks only at the short-run demand curve ends up where?
column2: Above the long-run monopoly price (OP1), since the short-run curve is less elastic above the current price.

column1: Cloze: Coase (1937) argues that 'the notion of a long-run demand curve is in the nature of a {{c1::fiction}}'.
column2: fiction — because price changes provoke experiments with substitutes that shift demand

column1: Coase's examples of price rises permanently lowering demand?
column2: Greek currant monopoly → people tried raisins; Stevenson rubber restriction → reclaimed rubber research; also tin restriction schemes.

column1: Coase 1937: short-run vs long-run outcome of monopoly compared with Robinson?
column2: At first less restriction than Robinson's construction suggests; in the long run, as demand becomes lower and more elastic, more restriction.

column1: Whose phrase 'The best of all monopoly profits is a quiet life!' does Coase use, and to what end?
column2: Hicks (Econometrica 1935); Coase argues it keeps price below the profit-maximising level and slows invention and progress.

column1: Don't confuse: Coase's 1937 RES article in this set vs 'The Nature of the Firm'?
column2: #64 is 'Some Notes on Monopoly Price' (RES, Oct 1937). 'The Nature of the Firm' (Economica, Nov 1937) is not in the folder.

column1: Burns 1937: what should be the central objective of industry studies?
column2: The analysis (generalised explanation) of the behaviour of prices, aimed at improving general price theory.

column1: Burns 1937: the three categories of 'competitive individualism' now unsuitable?
column2: The entrepreneur, the competitive market, and the rational individual buyer.

column1: What does Burns mean by the 'disintegration of the entrepreneur'?
column2: Functions once under 'a single hat' — risking capital and making price/production policy — are dispersed within the corporation (ownership vs control) and via contracts.

column1: Burns 1937: three relocations of function accompanying the entrepreneur's disintegration?
column2: (1) Larger scale relative to markets; (2) changed integration of activities (reintegration); (3) transfer of appraising utilities from buyer to seller (sales promotion).

column1: Cloze: Burns: with sales promotion, the tendency toward normal profits works out partly through the {{c1::raising of costs}}, not falling prices.
column2: raising of costs

column1: Burns 1937: example of an industry where geographical market definition leads to basing-point pricing?
column2: Cement — many plants nationally but few competing sellers in each area, with overlapping 'chain' markets.

column1: Burns 1937 presented where and when?
column2: Round table of the American Economic Association, Chicago, December 1936; published JPE October 1937.

column1: Burns 1937: why does integration complicate price analysis?
column2: It blurs costs: costs at each stage and of different products require arbitrary allocations (e.g. of management), and it removes the market as a check on efficiency.

column1: Kaldor 1938: what is the 'heart of the whole matter' that makes MR important?
column2: The relation of price to marginal cost, which depends on demand elasticity at equilibrium, i.e. on the position of MR.

column1: Kaldor 1938: Chamberlin's 'fundamental' confusion on numbers of firms?
column2: Confusing slope with elasticity: a leftward shift with unchanged slope still raises elasticity, moving price toward marginal cost.

column1: Cloze: For Kaldor (1938), the slope of a demand curve, though not its elasticity, is a matter of the {{c1::scale of drawing}}.
column2: scale of drawing

column1: Kaldor 1938 on Chamberlin's 'infinite number of infinitesimal firms' objection?
column2: Pure competition arrives once producers take price as given and set P = MC; it does not require infinitely many firms.

column1: What did Kaldor (1938) regard as Chamberlin's 'great achievement', now disclaimed?
column2: Showing that monopoly-like situations can coexist with full freedom of entry — monopoly without privilege, from economies of scale and small demand per variety.

column1: Kaldor 1938 example contrasting privilege vs scale-based monopoly?
column2: The company store in a company town (privilege) vs Henry Ford (economies of large-scale production).

column1: Kaldor's 1938 terminological proposal?
column2: 'Monopoly' = institutional privilege; 'imperfect competition' = limitation from economies of scale with free entry; 'monopolistic competition' = limitation from restriction of entry.

column1: Which paper said Chamberlin had 'fallen a victim to' sellers' tendency and 'is trying to differentiate his product too far'?
column2: Kaldor, 'Professor Chamberlin on Monopolistic and Imperfect Competition', QJE May 1938.

column1: Machlup 1939: four groups for whom a theory may be 'practical'?
column2: Pure theorist, applied analyst, government official (political economist), businessman — only applied analysis and government control count here.

column1: What is 'polypoly' (Machlup)?
column2: A market where very many sellers compete, each believing rivals won't react to what he does.

column1: Machlup 1939: how is oligopoly defined?
column2: Subjectively — the seller consciously includes in his calculations the reactions he expects from rivals.

column1: Machlup 1939: two consequences of vague oligopolistic conjectures?
column2: Price rigidity and increased selling costs.

column1: Machlup 1939: polypoly with differentiated products vs pure competition?
column2: He surmises prices and output would not be much different — and such markets usually break into small oligopolistic groups.

column1: Cloze: Machlup says the existence of so much oligopoly is a bad blow for {{c1::general equilibrium theory}}.
column2: general equilibrium theory

column1: What did Machlup conclude from his ten years as an industry executive?
column2: Neither differentiation nor oligopoly much affected decisions (demand was highly elastic); sensible businessmen act as economists suppose, though they rationalise misleadingly.

column1: Why does Machlup invoke Mr. Firestone's breakfast?
column2: Oligopoly prices depend on decisions of a few individuals, so theory faces limits that mass (law-of-large-numbers) behaviour does not.

column1: Date card: Machlup's AER evaluation — presented when?
column2: AEA Round Table, Detroit, 29 Dec 1938; published AER June 1939.
